title: The Happiness Bump of Marriage
text:
Does getting married make people happier for good? Earlier surveys had found married people happier than single people, but that could simply mean happier people are more likely to marry. To track individuals over time, Richard Lucas, Andrew Clark, Yannis Georgellis and Ed Diener turned to the German Socio-Economic Panel, a survey that had asked the same people about their life satisfaction every year for fifteen years.

Among more than 24,000 people, they followed those who married during the study and those who lost a spouse. For the people who married, life satisfaction rose in the years leading up to the wedding and peaked around it. Then, on average, it drifted back to roughly where it had been before, within a couple of years. People seemed to adapt to marriage, as they adapt to many good things.

The average hid wide differences. Some people stayed happier long after marrying; others ended up less happy than before. Widowhood was different: satisfaction fell sharply, and on average people recovered only slowly and not completely, even years later.

The study added nuance to the idea that each person has a fixed happiness set point. Adaptation is common, but it is neither complete nor the same for everyone.
lesson: A wedding does not deliver lasting happiness by itself. What follows, the daily care of the relationship, decides whether the glow fades or grows.
people: Richard Lucas, Andrew Clark, Yannis Georgellis, Ed Diener
source: Lucas, R. E., Clark, A. E., Georgellis, Y., and Diener, E. (2003). Reexamining adaptation and the set point model of happiness: Reactions to changes in marital status. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(3), 527-539.
